"When God's carpet is spread out and laid flat, and its rugs and cushions are brought near for its people."

Al-Kalbī said: they are cushions arranged one beside another.

Muqātil said: they are cushions arranged upon the carpets (ṭanāfis).

As for "zarābī" (rugs), it means spreads and carpets (ṭanāfis), and its singular is "zarība," according to the consensus of all linguists and commentators.

And "mabthūtha" (spread out) means laid out and spread.

Then reflect on the wondrous wisdom in the mountains, which the ignorant and heedless person considers a superfluous part of the earth, with no need for it, though in them are benefits that none can count except their Creator and the one who set them firmly in place. In the hadith of the conversion of Dimam ibn Tha'laba, he said to the Prophet: "Has God, who set up the mountains and deposited in them benefits, commanded you to do such-and-such?" He said: "O God, yes."

Among their benefits: snow falls upon them and remains on their peaks, available as drink for people until it melts. It was made to melt gradually, little by little, so that from it come the abundant torrents, and from it flow the rivers and valleys, and there grow in the meadows, lowlands and hills all kinds of plants, fruits and medicines that cannot be found in the plains and sands. Had it not been for the mountains, the snow would have fallen upon the surface of the earth, melted all at once and flowed in one rush, so it would have been lost when people needed it, and its sudden melting would have produced floods that destroy whatever they pass over, harming people with a harm that cannot be averted or repelled.

Among their benefits are the caves, grottoes and strongholds on their summits and peaks, which hold the place of fortresses and citadels.

They are also shelters for people and animals.

Among their benefits is what is hewn from their stones for buildings of various kinds, for millstones and other things.

Among their benefits are the minerals found in them of various kinds: gold, silver, copper, iron, lead, chrysolite and emerald, and many more kinds of minerals that human beings cannot fully identify in detail. Indeed, among them there are things of which a small amount is worth and benefits more than gold many times over.

In them are benefits that none knows except their Originator and Creator, glory be to Him.

Among their benefits also is that they repel violent winds and break their force, so that they do not allow them to strike what is beneath them; for this reason, those who dwell beneath them are safe from the great, harmful winds.

Among their benefits also is that they hold back floods from them when they are in their courses, turning them away to the right and to the left; without them, floods would ravage whatever they pass through, so they serve them as a dam and a shelter.

Among their benefits is that they are landmarks by which one is guided on the roads; they hold the place of the markers set up to guide to the paths. For this reason God called them landmarks, saying: ﴿And among His signs are the ships in the sea like landmarks﴾

So "al-jawari" (the ships) and "al-a'lam" (the mountains), whose singular is "'alam."

al-Khansa' said:

"Indeed Sakhr is one whom the guided take as a guide, as if he were a landmark with a fire on its top."

So she called the mountain an "'alam" from "'alama" (sign) and "zuhur" (prominence).

Among their benefits also is what grows in them of herbs and medicines that do not exist in the plains and sands, just as what grows in the plains and sands does not grow like it in the mountains. In each of these and those there are benefits and wisdoms that none encompasses except the All-Creator, the All-Knowing.

Among their benefits is that they are fortresses against enemies, in which the servants of God take refuge from their enemies, just as they fortify themselves with citadels; indeed they are more eloquent and more secure than many citadels and cities.

Among their benefits is what God Most High mentioned in His Book, that He made them as pegs for the earth, holding it firm, and as firm mountains (rawasi), like the anchors of ships; and how great a benefit and wisdom that is.

Furthermore, if you reflect on their wondrous, marvelous creation in this arrangement, you will find it in the utmost conformity with wisdom. For if they were long and stretched out like a wall, it would be impossible to climb them or benefit from them, and they would screen the sun and air from people, so they could not benefit from them. And if they were spread over the surface of the earth, they would constrict fields and dwellings on them, fill up the plain, and people would not gain from them the benefit of fortification, caves and shelters; and they would not shield them from winds, nor hold back floods. And if they were made round, in the shape of a sphere, people could not climb them, and they would not gain full benefit from them. So the most fitting shape and arrangement for them, most suited to them and most conducive to the good, is this shape upon which they were set.

God, glory be to Him, has indeed called us in His Book to contemplate them and how they were created, saying: ﴿Do they not look at the camel, how it was created? And at the sky, how it was raised? And at the mountains, how they were set up? And at the earth, how it was spread out?﴾

So their creation and their benefits are among the greatest proofs of the power of their Fashioner, Originator, of His knowledge, wisdom and oneness.

Moreover, they glorify Him with His praise, humble themselves before Him, prostrate, split open and descend out of fear of Him. They are the ones who feared their Lord, Originator and Creator despite their hardness and great size, when the trust was offered to them and they were afraid to bear it.

Among them is the mountain upon which God spoke to Moses, His interlocutor and confidant.

Among them is the mountain upon which His Lord manifested Himself, so it crumbled and was leveled to dust.

Among them is the mountain which God made beloved to His Messenger and his Companions, and which the Messenger of God and his Companions love.

Among them are the two mountains which God made as a sign on behalf of His Prophet, placing aṣ-Ṣafā at the foot of one of them and al-Marwa at the foot of the other, and prescribed for His servants the sa'y (running) between them, making it one of their rites and acts of worship.

Among them is the Mountain of Mercy, upon which the plain of 'Arafat is set.

How many sins are forgiven there, how many slips of speech and pardoned lapses, needs fulfilled, distresses relieved, afflictions lifted, blessings renewed, happiness gained and misery erased! Glory be to God for that mountain and what descends upon it of mercy and pardon for great sins.

How could it not be, when it is the mountain singled out for that greatest gathering and most noble delegation, who came from every deep ravine, standing before their Lord, humbled before His greatness, submissive before His might, dishevelled and dusty, with their heads bare, seeking the removal of their stumbles and asking Him for their needs; then He draws near to them and boasts of them to the angels.

So glory be to that mountain and to what descends upon it of mercy and forgiveness of great sins.

Among them is Mount Hira, where the Messenger of God used to seclude himself with his Lord until God honored him with His message while he was in its cave. It is the mountain from which light poured out over the regions of the world, and it boasts over the other mountains, and it has every right to do so.

Glory be to Him who singles out with His mercy and honor whom He wills, of mountains and of men: He made some mountains magnets for hearts, as if they were made of it; hearts yearn toward them whenever they remember them, and are drawn to them, just as He singles out from among men whom He honors and completes His blessing upon, placing His love upon him, so that He loves him, makes him beloved to His angels and His believing servants, and places acceptance for him on earth among them.

And when you reflect upon the lands, you will find them
"They are wretched as men are wretched, and they are happy as men are happy."

So leave aside that particular mountain, the mountain of such-and-such a clan, and that mountain of such-and-such:

"Take what you see and leave what you have only heard of;
in the sunrise, you have no need of Saturn."

This is the state of the mountains, which are hard stone, yet this is their softness and their fear, and their crumbling from the majesty and greatness of their Lord. Their Fashioner and Creator has informed us about them that, had He sent down His speech upon them, they would have humbled themselves and split apart out of fear of God.

How strange it is, then, that a lump of flesh is harder than these mountains: the verses of God are recited to it, and its Lord, blessed and exalted, is mentioned, yet it does not soften, nor humble itself, nor turn back in repentance. It is no wonder for God, Mighty and Majestic, nor is it contrary to His wisdom, that He should create for such a heart a fire to melt it, since it did not soften by His speech, His remembrance, His warnings and His admonitions. Whoever's heart does not soften for God in this abode, nor turns to Him, nor is melted by His love and weeping out of fear of Him, let him enjoy a little, for before him is the Greatest Melter, and he will return to the world of the unseen and the witnessed, where he will see and know.

So she called the mountain an "'alam" from "'alama" (sign) and "zuhur" (prominence).

Among their benefits also is what grows in them of herbs and medicines that do not exist in the plains and sands, just as what grows in the plains and sands does not grow like it in the mountains. In each of these and those there are benefits and wisdoms that none encompasses except the All-Creator, the All-Knowing.

Among their benefits is that they are fortresses against enemies, in which the servants of God take refuge from their enemies, just as they fortify themselves with citadels; indeed they are more eloquent and more secure than many citadels and cities.

Among their benefits is what God Most High mentioned in His Book, that He made them as pegs for the earth, holding it firm, and as firm mountains (rawasi), like the anchors of ships; and how great a benefit and wisdom that is.

Furthermore, if you reflect on their wondrous, marvelous creation in this arrangement, you will find it in the utmost conformity with wisdom. For if they were long and stretched out like a wall, it would be impossible to climb them or benefit from them, and they would screen the sun and air from people, so they could not benefit from them. And if they were spread over the surface of the earth, they would constrict fields and dwellings on them, fill up the plain, and people would not gain from them the benefit of fortification, caves and shelters; and they would not shield them from winds, nor hold back floods. And if they were made round, in the shape of a sphere, people could not climb them, and they would not gain full benefit from them. So the most fitting shape and arrangement for them, most suited to them and most conducive to the good, is this shape upon which they were set.

God, glory be to Him, has indeed called us in His Book to contemplate them and how they were created, saying: ﴿Do they not look at the camel, how it was created? And at the sky, how it was raised? And at the mountains, how they were set up? And at the earth, how it was spread out?﴾

So their creation and their benefits are among the greatest proofs of the power of their Fashioner, Originator, of His knowledge, wisdom and oneness.

Moreover, they glorify Him with His praise, humble themselves before Him, prostrate, split open and descend out of fear of Him. They are the ones who feared their Lord, Originator and Creator despite their hardness and great size, when the trust was offered to them and they were afraid to bear it.

Among them is the mountain upon which God spoke to Moses, His interlocutor and confidant.

Among them is the mountain upon which His Lord manifested Himself, so it crumbled and was leveled to dust.

Among them is the mountain which God made beloved to His Messenger and his Companions, and which the Messenger of God and his Companions love.

Among them are the two mountains which God made as a sign on behalf of His Prophet, placing aṣ-Ṣafā at the foot of one of them and al-Marwa at the foot of the other, and prescribed for His servants the sa'y (running) between them, making it one of their rites and acts of worship.

Among them is the Mountain of Mercy, upon which the plain of 'Arafat is set.

How many sins are forgiven there, how many slips of speech and pardoned lapses, needs fulfilled, distresses relieved, afflictions lifted, blessings renewed, happiness gained and misery erased! Glory be to God for that mountain and what descends upon it of mercy and pardon for great sins.

How could it not be, when it is the mountain singled out for that greatest gathering and most noble delegation, who came from every deep ravine, standing before their Lord, humbled before His greatness, submissive before His might, dishevelled and dusty, with their heads bare, seeking the removal of their stumbles and asking Him for their needs; then He draws near to them and boasts of them to the angels.

So glory be to that mountain and to what descends upon it of mercy and forgiveness of great sins.

Among them is Mount Hira, where the Messenger of God used to seclude himself with his Lord until God honored him with His message while he was in its cave. It is the mountain from which light poured out over the regions of the world, and it boasts over the other mountains, and it has every right to do so.

Glory be to Him who singles out with His mercy and honor whom He wills, of mountains and of men: He made some mountains magnets for hearts, as if they were made of it; hearts yearn toward them whenever they remember them, and are drawn to them, just as He singles out from among men whom He honors and completes His blessing upon, placing His love upon him, so that He loves him, makes him beloved to His angels and His believing servants, and places acceptance for him on earth among them.

And when you reflect upon the lands, you will find them
"They are wretched as men are wretched, and they are happy as men are happy."

So leave aside that particular mountain, the mountain of such-and-such a clan, and that mountain of such-and-such:

"Take what you see and leave what you have only heard of;
in the sunrise, you have no need of Saturn."

This is the state of the mountains, which are hard stone, yet this is their softness and their fear, and their crumbling from the majesty and greatness of their Lord. Their Fashioner and Creator has informed us about them that, had He sent down His speech upon them, they would have humbled themselves and split apart out of fear of God.

How strange it is, then, that a lump of flesh is harder than these mountains: the verses of God are recited to it, and its Lord, blessed and exalted, is mentioned, yet it does not soften, nor humble itself, nor turn back in repentance. It is no wonder for God, Mighty and Majestic, nor is it contrary to His wisdom, that He should create for such a heart a fire to melt it, since it did not soften by His speech, His remembrance, His warnings and His admonitions. Whoever's heart does not soften for God in this abode, nor turns to Him, nor is melted by His love and weeping out of fear of Him, let him enjoy a little, for before him is the Greatest Melter, and he will return to the world of the unseen and the witnessed, where he will see and know.

(Fa'idah)

Another expression for the disjunctive exception (al-istithna' al-munqati', "the discontinuous exception") is that it is disjunctive from what precedes it, either in its ruling (al-'amal) or in its inclusion of the same category (tanawul).

Disjunctive in inclusion: "The people came, except a donkey."

Disjunctive in ruling: such as the words of God Most High: ﴿You are not over them a controller (22). Except for him who turns away and disbelieves (23), then God will punish him with the greatest punishment (24).﴾

This is a disjunctive exception with a whole clause (bi-jumlah).

So said Ibn Kharoof and others.

They took (man) as the subject (mubtada') and (yu'adhdhibuhu) as its predicate, and the fa' entered because the subject was given the meaning of a conditional (shart).

Ibn al-Qayyim also said in (Bada'i' al-Fawa'id):

The words of God Most High: ﴿You are not over them a controller, except for him who turns away and disbelieves, then God will punish him with the greatest punishment.﴾

This is disjunctive, but not in the sense mentioned by Ibn Kharoof, namely that the excepted item is an independent clause. It is disjunctive in another respect: the intent is not to establish control over the disbelievers, for God Most High sent him only as a warner and a conveyor of the messages of his Lord. Whoever obeys him has Paradise, and whoever disobeys him has the Fire. God Most High says: ﴿But if they turn away, We have not sent you as a watcher over them; your duty is only to convey (the message)﴾, and He says: ﴿Say: O mankind, the truth has come to you from your Lord. So whoever is guided, it is only for his own soul that he is guided; and whoever goes astray, it is only against it that he goes astray. And I am not a guardian over you.﴾

The exegetes said: The meaning is that you were not sent as one who holds power over them, a dominant compeller, a tyrant like kings; rather, you are My servant and My messenger who conveys My messages.

Whoever obeys you has Paradise, and whoever disobeys you has the Fire.

What makes this clear is that those addressed by this address are the disbelievers, so it is not valid for them to be the excepted ones.

(Fa'idah)

(Exhortation)

Since they were created, people have never ceased to be travelers, and they have no place to set down their saddlebags except in Paradise or in Hellfire.

The intelligent person knows that travel is founded on hardship and the riding of dangers.

It is customary and impossible that one should seek in it bliss, pleasure, and comfort; rather, that comes only after the journey has ended.

It is known that every step of a foot, and every moment of the moments of the journey, does not stand still, and the one held responsible (al-mukallaf) does not stand still either.

It has been established that he is a traveler in the state in which the traveler must be, namely preparing the provision that delivers him (al-mūṣil).

And when he halts, or sleeps, or rests, it is with his foot poised for setting out again.
